searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's, one left unspent for the run's shared allowance. The shared search went to the demarcation of Colares and Carcavelos (Decreto-Lei 246/94 on the Diário da República, the Carta de Lei of 18 September 1908 confirming the decree of 10 May 1907). Two searches of the Adega's record were restricted to the bodies' domains (the Diário da República and the IVV) and one to the Adega's own; one of the Romeira's to sogrape.com and Garrafeira Nacional; one of Villa Oeiras's to the IVV and the Diário da República. The rest went to the open web with the author's sources blocked where the account had to be independent (Decantalo, Decanter, Salt of Portugal, Hedonism, Leon and Son, Shrine to the Vine, Liberty Wines, The Wine Society, Wine Spectator, Agroportal, The Drinks Business, Infovini, the council's pages, villaoeiras.com, Haus Alpenz, Euronews, Alt Wines, Amathus, Wines of Portugal, Winetourism, The Yeatman, Wine Trail Traveler). Writers' own sites that came up (a wiki under a writer's name, two critics' sites, a blogger's page and an article with its author in the address) were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the laws and their years, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to what a guest would be told most often and what most needed a second source: the appellation on each label, the rule of the sand at Colares, the years of the story (1931, 1934, 1994, 1808, 1911, 2019, the replanting at Oeiras, the purchase at Alenquer), then to the making, then to the other wines.

Where a governing text settled a point it was followed (the portaria of 12 March 2021 for the soils of Colares, the IVV for the ageing of Carcavelos, Decreto-Lei 235/94 and 246/94 for the monopoly and the demarcation); where accounts disagreed and none was primary, the field was widened (Prova Régia's appellation by vintage, the replanting in the 1980s) or hedged (by most accounts in 1990); where a fact rested on one account and the refuter found it nowhere, it was cut (the yeasts at Viúva Gomes, the skin contact of Prova Régia, the Espumante Bruto, the Viticultores cask, the plain red of Syrah alone).

tested: The founding and the claim: Montepio, Winalist, Fenadegas and Cellartours give 1931; the Adega's own site, Montepio and Fenadegas call it the oldest wine co-operative in Portugal. Borne out, the claim kept as the Adega's own.

The monopoly: the preamble of Decreto-Lei 235/94 (vLex) binds the region to the Adega by Decreto-Lei 24 500 of 1934 and a statute of 1941, the Adega compulsory for wine sold as Colares, and recalls that Lei 8/85 asked its return to a winemaking role; Decreto-Lei 246/94 gave the new statutes of Carcavelos and Colares. Borne out: the 1930s, some six decades, the decree of 15 September 1994.
The demarcation: Decreto-Lei 246/94 gives the decree of 10 May 1907 confirmed by the Carta de Lei of 18 September 1908; the Adega's own page gives a demarcated region since 1908. Borne out.

The making: Tesouros de Baco (the 2017, bottled in February 2025), Cave Lusa (the 2016), Garrafeira Venceslau (the 2012) and Auchan (the 2020) give five years, first in large vats of exotic wood and then in small oak casks; Público's review of the 2006 gives fermentation in stainless steel; an older note on the 2000 gave four years with the order reversed. The figure borne out, the vessels and the steel added.

The soil rule: the portaria of 12 March 2021 in the Diário da República names two recommended soils for Colares, chão de areia and chão rijo, keeps the old ungrafted planting in the sand and lets a Colares take up to 20 per cent of wine from chão rijo vineyards; a search of the DOC's rules agrees, and the Adega's Chão Rijo is a regional wine. Not borne out: the trap and the wine question's explanation said wine of the clay cannot be Colares.
Arenae Malvasia on the Adega's own shop page, and the half litre bottle on Auchan's listing beside the author's merchants. Borne out.

The questions: one right answer each, four reasons and four cellars, the explanations teaching the nearest wrong option. The house rules: the Adega's oenologist not named, no price (the Adega's shop prices met), no score, nothing volatile (its share of the region's growers and production met and not used), British, no dash.

changed.was: Made at the co-operative's cellar from its members' grapes, the wine is fermented on its skins and then aged in wood for years, about five in the vintages its merchants describe, the old Colares way, before it is bottled in half litre bottles and released.
changed.now: Made at the co-operative's cellar from its members' grapes, the wine is fermented on its skins in stainless steel and aged for about five years, first in large vats of exotic wood and then in smaller oak casks in the vintages of 2012 to 2020 its merchants describe, before it is bottled in half litre bottles.
changed.why: Four merchants' sheets give the two vessels in order and five years; Público gives the steel; the old Colares way said nothing a guest could keep.

open: The law that gave the Adega its sole right: Decreto-Lei 24 500 of 1934 by the preamble of Decreto-Lei 235/94, 1938 in other accounts; the record says the 1930s.
The claim of the oldest wine co-operative in Portugal rests on the Adega and two pages that repeat it; it is told as the Adega's own.
The order of the vessels before 2012: one note on the 2000 gave oak first and the vats of exotic wood after.

tested: The year: Sábado's Alma dos Vinhos de Lisboa and the parish council of Colares give 1808, the parish calling it one of the oldest cellars, possibly the oldest; Sábado names a founder and tells of his widow, with no dates, so neither is named. Borne out, kept as the house's own date.

The making, the author's sources blocked: Tourinto's sheets for the 1965 and 1969 give casks of Portuguese chestnut and mahogany, and whole bunches fermented in large wooden vats in those years; a critic's note on Wine-Searcher gives whole bunches in tank then trodden by foot for the 2017; no second account of the wine's own yeasts. The treading and the woods borne out, the yeasts cut.
The spelling: Vivino lists the wine as Viúva Gomes Collares Tinto, beside Decanter. Borne out.
The old vintages: Tourinto (1965, 1969) and Cave Lusa (1969). Borne out.

The other wines: the house's own home page gives the Viticultores as wines of local growers' grapes and its own, not on the sand, inside the bounds of the appellation without meeting its statute; Tourinto gives the red as a Vinho Regional Lisboa of Castelão, Ramisco and Touriga Nacional and the white as led by Malvasia de Colares. Not borne out: grapes from outside the appellation, and the cask rested on one sheet.

The questions: one right answer each, four label readings and four years; the spelling explanation no longer teaches the clay rule refuted in the Adega's record. The house rules: the father and son who keep the house not named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash.

changed.was: In 1808, as the house tells it, a cellar was built in the village of Almoçageme, under the Sintra hills, to make the wine of Colares, and the name the house has traded under means the widow Gomes. A century later, in 1908, Colares was demarcated: a strip of dune sand by the Atlantic where vines are planted down to the clay, out of phylloxera's reach. In 1931 the Adega Regional de Colares was founded to vinify the growers' grapes and vouch for the wine, and through the 1930s the law gave the co-operative the sole right to make Colares, so for some six decades the wine of every house, Viúva Gomes among them, began in its cellar. A decree of 1994 ended that framework, and the house makes its own Colares again, from its small plots and the vineyards of local growers: whole bunches trodden by foot, fermented with their own yeasts and aged for five years and more in casks of oak, chestnut and Brazilian mahogany. Its label keeps the old spelling, Collares. From its cellar the house has also released old vintages of the 1960s, and they show what Ramisco from the sand becomes with time: firm and alive after half a century. For a sommelier, it is the Colares to open when a guest asks what an old ungrafted European vine tastes like.

tested: The purchase: Público and Grandes Escolhas made it public on 4 January 2019, Grandes Escolhas saying it had run in the trade for a while; WineTrust and others give 2018. Changed to made public at the start of 2019.

The appellation: Brasil Vinhos (2020) gives Prova Régia as IG Lisboa then, with Sogrape hoping to take it to DOC Bucelas; Firstleaf lists the 2015 and BGWM the 2019 as Lisboa Arinto; Vinha lists the 2023 as Bucelas DOC, Radar a Bucelas labelled version beside a plain one, The Wine Society the 2024 as Bucelas; Garrafeira Nacional gives the region as Lisboa. Not borne out as Bucelas in every vintage.

The making, the author's sources blocked: a technical sheet of the 2022 (13 to 15 degrees Celsius), a sheet of the 2023 (14 to 16, after cold settling) and the importer's of the 2024 (16 to 18); three or four months on the fine lees with stirring on two sheets; no wood on any sheet. Borne out with the figures widened; the short skin contact and the pneumatic press, on one importer, cut.
Bucelas: the Loures council gives a decree of 3 March 1911; the Confraria do Arinto de Bucelas gives Arinto at least 75 per cent. Borne out.

Wellington: the Confraria, the Loures council and others tell the gift to George III, one calling him the regent; Wine Ventures and another tell George IV and the estate as his headquarters. Borne out as a story, the king left unnamed.

The dates of the estate: Sogrape's own material gives documents from 1218 and the morgado of 1703; Wine Ventures, the earlier producer, gives the morgado of Santa Catherina of 1703. Changed from the merchants' 1703 for the wine.

The other wines: Morgado de Santa Catherina on Sogrape's distribution site and the importer; Prova Régia Reserva, Arinto alone, on Garrafeira Nacional, Winehouse Portugal and Radar; the Espumante Bruto on one list only. Changed.

The spelling: Sogrape's distribution site and a regional paper (May 2026) give the new identity as Quinta da Romeyra; The Wine Society still lists the 2024 under Quinta da Romeira, so the label term was cut while the trap stands.

The questions: one right answer each, four vessels and four historic figures. The house rules: Sogrape's chief executive, quoted in Público, and the estate's winemaker not named; the seller told by no name; no price (suggested prices on Sogrape's pages met), no score, nothing volatile (the 75 of 130 hectares and the largest Arinto vineyard met and not used), British, no dash.

changed.was: Quinta da Romeira lies at Bucelas, just north of Lisbon; its owners trace its documents to the thirteenth century, and its merchants date its wine to 1703. During the Peninsular War, as the story is told, the Duke of Wellington (1769 to 1852) came to know the white wine of Bucelas and took it home to England for the king, and the name Prova Régia, royal approval, recalls that story. In 1911 Bucelas was demarcated as an appellation of white wine alone, with Arinto at its heart. Prova Régia, Arinto from the estate fermented in steel and kept away from oak, became the label by which British merchants knew the estate. At the start of 2019 Sogrape bought Quinta da Romeira, its first foothold in the Lisboa region, and it later took back the old spelling of the name, Romeyra, for the brand, which it presents as a new chapter for the Arinto of Bucelas. For a sommelier, Prova Régia is the plain lesson of Bucelas: a dry, saline white of one grape from the edge of the capital, to pour with the fish course.
changed.now: Quinta da Romeira lies at Bucelas, just north of Lisbon; its owners trace its documents to 1218, and the morgado of Santa Catherina, the entailed estate it belonged to, to 1703. tested: The grapes: Portugal Vineyards, Garrafinhas, Tourinto and other merchants give Arinto, Galego Dourado and Ratinho. Borne out.

The making: a sheet reproduced by a merchant gives spirit at 77 per cent from Lourinhã added midway through the fermentation; most merchants give fifteen years on average in Portuguese and French oak; the IVV's specification asks two years in wood and six months in bottle, and the portaria of 12 March 2021 gives 24 months in wood. Borne out.

Superior and 15 Anos: Portugal Vineyards, Garrafinhas, Tourinto and others list one wine, Villa Oeiras Superior 15 Anos, so the author's doubt is answered: one wine. The replanting: the house's account and a book of 1990 give 1983, under the station's director; a paper of 2005 gives four new vineyards in 1984 at the Quintas do Marquês, dos Pesos, da Ribeira and da Samarra; Grandes Escolhas gives the station's first vines in 1985. changed.was: Carcavelos is the fortified wine of the coast west of Lisbon, and the Marquis of Pombal (1699 to 1782), the minister who rebuilt Lisbon after the earthquake of 1755, made it on his family estate at Oeiras, from 1752 by the council's account. The appellation was demarcated in 1908, but oidium, mildew and phylloxera had already struck its vines, and through the twentieth century the villas, hotels and suburbs of the growing city covered its vineyards, until only two producers were left. In 1983 the national agronomy station, the Estação Agronómica Nacional, replanted vines on the Marquis's old estate, and the Oeiras council later joined it in a partnership to save the wine. The council created the brand Villa Oeiras, equipped a new cellar at Casal da Manteiga, extended the vineyard and recovered the palace's old wine cellar in 2012. Its Carcavelos is made in the modern way, the fermentation stopped with grape spirit, where the nineteenth century had fermented the wine dry and fortified it with vinho abafado, and it is aged for years in Portuguese and French oak. To a sommelier, Villa Oeiras is the revival of Carcavelos in a glass: a fortified wine of white grapes, aged in wood, from an appellation the city almost erased.

changed.was: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro lies near Alenquer, in the hills north of Lisbon, some twenty kilometres from the Atlantic and open to its steady wind. In the late 1980s the estate was bought by a gastronome with a passion for the wines of the Rhône, and its vineyards were planted mostly with Syrah and Viognier, the grapes of the northern Rhône. The new estate made its opening wine with the 1997 vintage. The Reserva, Syrah from several plots fermented with a few per cent of Viognier as Côte-Rôtie does, and aged in French oak, became the estate's flagship, the wine with which it set out to show what Syrah can do in the Atlantic hills of Lisboa. From the 2006 harvest the estate began its conversion to organic farming, with new labels for a new phase of its history, and its vineyards are certified organic. The Reserva is labelled Vinho Regional Lisboa rather than DOC Alenquer. For a sommelier, it is the Portuguese Syrah to pour beside a northern Rhône red: perfumed, peppery and supple, from vines a short drive from the capital.
